'''Gábor Laurenczy''' is a [[Hungary|Hungarian]]-[[Switzerland|Swiss]] [[chemist]] and [[Academic staff|academic]]. He is a [[Professor]] [[Emeritus]] at the [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne]]. He is academician, External Member of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mta.hu/koztestuleti_tagok?PersonId=9665 |title=Az MTA köztestületének tagjai}}</ref><ref name=tyur>{{Cite web|url=https://people.epfl.ch/gabor.laurenczy|title=EPFL People – Gabor Laurenczy|website=EPFL People}}</ref>

Laurenczy's research interests lie in the field of [[reaction kinetics]], primarily focusing on [[hydrogen storage]], [[hydrogenation]] and catalytic activation of small [[molecules]]. He is the recipient of the Rudolf Fabinyi Memorial Prize by The Hungarian [[Chemical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mke.org.hu/en/prizes/honoured-individuals/fabinyi-rudolf-emlrem-mainmenu-149.html|title=Fabinyi Rudolf Emlékérem díjazottjai}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://actu.epfl.ch/news/double-honors-for-gabor-laurenczy-3/|title=Double honors for Gabor Laurenczy|first=Nik|last=Papageorgiou|date=May 5, 2022}}</ref>

==Education==
Laurenczy earned a [[Master's degree]] in Chemistry from Kossuth University (Debrecen, Hungary) in 1978. Subsequently, he pursued his [[Ph.D.]] in [[Inorganic Chemistry]] at the same institution, completing it in 1980.<ref name=tyur/>

==Career==
Laurenczy began his academic career in 1984 in Kossuth University as an [[assistant professor]]. In 1985 he moved to Switzerland (UNIL). In 1991, he made his [[habilitation]] (Hungarian Academy of Sciences, Budapest). In the same year, he was appointed as Maître Assistant at the [[University of Lausanne]], followed by an appointment as a maître d'enseignement et de recherche at the same institution in 1997. He also served as the [[Visiting scholar|visiting professor]] at the Université de Bourgogne in 2007. In 2010, he was appointed as professor at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, a role that he served until 2019. As of 2019, he is the professor emeritus at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne. In 2022, he was elected as an External Member of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences.<ref name=tyur/>

==Research==
Laurenczy is most known for his works on [[hydrogen]] storage & generation, catalytic activation of small molecules, the development of medium and high-pressure equipment, [[iron]] catalysts,<ref>{{Cite journal|title=A well-defined iron catalyst for the reduction of bicarbonates and carbon dioxide to formates, alkyl formates, and formamides|first1=Christopher|last1=Federsel|first2=Albert|last2=Boddien|first3=Ralf|last3=Jackstell|first4=Reiko|last4=Jennerjahn|first5=Paul J.|last5=Dyson|first6=Rosario|last6=Scopelliti|first7=Gabor|last7=Laurenczy|first8=Matthias|last8=Beller|date=December 10, 2010|journal= Angewandte Chemie International Edition|volume=49|issue=50|pages=9777–9780|doi=10.1002/anie.201004263|pmid=21069647}}</ref> and reactions with water-soluble compounds.<ref name=ttp/> He holds patents to numerous projects including ''[[Hydrogen production]] from formic acid''<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/211674?ln=en|title=Hydrogen production from formic acid|editor-first1=Gabor|editor-last1=Laurenczy|editor-first2=Celine|editor-last2=Fellay|editor-first3=Paul|editor-last3=Dyson|date=June 22, 2008}}</ref> and ''Direct [[carbon dioxide]] [[hydrogenation]] to [[formic acid]] in acidic media''. In addition, he has authored numerous publications, including book chapters and articles in peer-reviewed journals.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=vfKg8D8AAAAJ&view_op=list_works&sortby=pubdate|title=Gabor Laurenczy|website=scholar.google.com}}</ref>

Lauranczy's research on the Hydrogenation of compounds has focused on developing new catalysts,<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0020169300801784|title=The binding of dinitrogen to ruthenium(II) in aqueous solution|first1=Gábor|last1=Laurenczy|first2=Lothar|last2=Helm|first3=André E.|last3=Merbach|first4=Andreas|last4=Ludi|date=November 15, 1991|journal=Inorganica Chimica Acta|volume=189|issue=2|pages=131–133|doi=10.1016/S0020-1693(00)80178-4|url-access=subscription}}</ref> elucidating reaction mechanisms,<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ejic.201900344|title=A Precious Catalyst: Rhodium-Catalyzed Formic Acid Dehydrogenation in Water|first1=Cornel|last1=Fink|first2=Gábor|last2=Laurenczy|date=May 15, 2019|journal=European Journal of Inorganic Chemistry|volume=2019|issue=18|pages=2381–2387|doi=10.1002/ejic.201900344|s2cid=145890300 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> optimizing processes, overcoming challenges in hydrogenating specific substrates, and enabling selective transformations. He evaluated the effectiveness of hydrido-ruthenium(II) complexes as catalysts in hydrogenation reactions<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ic000200b|title=Formation and Laurenczy's hydrogen storage research has led to the development of hydrogen storage technologies.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2013/cc/c3cc43836h|title=Hydrogen storage: beyond conventional methods|first1=Andrew F.|last1=Dalebrook|first2=Weijia|last2=Gan|first3=Martin|last3=Grasemann|first4=Séverine|last4=Moret|first5=Gábor|last5=Laurenczy|date=September 5, 2013|journal=Chemical Communications|volume=49|issue=78|pages=8735–8751|doi=10.1039/C3CC43836H|pmid=23964360 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> He investigated the immobilization of a highly efficient homogeneous catalyst used in the formic acid decomposition process<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Selective formic acid decomposition for high-pressure hydrogen generation: a mechanistic study|first1=Céline|last1=Fellay|first2=Ning|last2=Yan|first3=Paul J.|last3=Dyson|first4=Gábor|last4=Laurenczy|date=June 22, 2009|journal=Chemistry: A European Journal|volume=15|issue=15|pages=3752–3760|doi=10.1002/chem.200801824|pmid=19229942|doi-access=free}}</ref> to produce hydrogen<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/264645848|title=Heterogeneous Silica-Supported Ruthenium Phosphine Catalysts for Selective Formic Acid Decomposition|last1=Gan|first1= Weijia|last2= Dyson|first2= J. Paul|last3= Laurenczy|first3= Gábor|journal= ChemCatChem|date=2013|volume= 5|pages=3124–3130}}</ref> and carbon dioxide and outlined different methods employed to immobilize the catalyst, ruthenium-TPPTS,<ref name=ttp>{{Cite journal|title=A viable hydrogen-storage system based on selective formic acid decomposition with a ruthenium catalyst|first1=Céline|last1=Fellay|first2=Paul J.|last2=Dyson|first3=Gábor|last3=Laurenczy|date=June 22, 2008|journal= Angewandte Chemie International Edition|volume=47|issue=21|pages=3966–3968|doi=10.1002/anie.200800320|pmid=18393267}}</ref> including ion exchange, coordination, and physical absorption techniques.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/43651980|title=Hydrogen storage and delivery: Immobilization of a highly active homogeneous catalyst for the decomposition of formic acid to hydrogen and carbon dioxide|last1=Gan|first1= Weijia|last2=Dyson|first2= J. ===High pressure kinetic studies===
During his investigation of the Bray reaction in enclosed environments and the influence of elevated pressure on the reaction, Laurenczy discovered that oxygen acts as an independent species and demonstrated that subjecting the reaction to high pressure (2000 bar) induced significant oscillation changes.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/j100071a004|title=Effect of High Pressure on the Bray Reaction|first1=Gabor|last1=Laurenczy|first2=Mihaly T.|last2=Beck|date=May 22, 1994|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry|volume=98|issue=20|pages=5188–5189|doi=10.1021/j100071a004|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Focusing on the stopped-flow technique, he conducted research on the interactions between specific divalent [[transition metal]] ions<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0020169300923570|title=Monocomplex formation and dissociation of some first row divalent transition metal ions with 2-chloro-1,10-phenanthroline by the high-pressure stopped-flow technique|first1=Gábor|last1=Laurenczy|first2=Pascal|last2=Bugnon|first3=André E.|last3=Merbach|date=August 1, 1992|journal=Inorganica Chimica Acta|volume=198-200|pages=159–164|doi=10.1016/S0020-1693(00)92357-0|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and also developed a high-pressure stopped-flow spectrometer capable of studying rapid reactions using absorbance and fluorescence detection.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=High-pressure stopped-flow spectrometer for kinetic studies of fast reactions by absorbance and fluorescence detection|first1=P.|last1=Bugnon|first2=G.|last2=Laurenczy|first3=Y.|last3=Ducommun|first4=P. Y.|last4=Sauvageat|first5=A. E.|last5=Merbach|first6=R.|last6=Ith|first7=R.|last7=Tschanz|first8=M.|last8=Doludda|first9=R.|last9=Bergbauer|first10=E.|last10=Grell|date=September 1, 1996|journal=Analytical Chemistry|volume=68|issue=17|pages=3045–3049|doi=10.1021/ac960382k|pmid=21619372}}</ref> In related research, his study established the role of the dimeric form of 1-methoxy-3-methyl carbonatotetrabutyldistannoxane as an intermediate in synthesizing dimethyl carbonate, while also highlighting the potential existence of a novel trinuclear di-n-butyltin(IV) compound, possibly derived from the organometallic precursor n-Bu<sub>2</sub>Sn(OCH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022328X11001069|title=Di-n-butyltin(IV)-catalyzed dimethyl carbonate synthesis from carbon dioxide and methanol: An in situ high pressure 119Sn{1H} NMR spectroscopic study|first1=Gábor|last1=Laurenczy|first2=Michel|last2=Picquet|first3=Laurent|last3=Plasseraud|date=May 1, 2011|journal=Journal of Organometallic Chemistry|volume=696|issue=9|pages=1904–1909|doi=10.1016/j.jorganchem.2011.02.010|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In his investigation of the catalytic capability of a uniform iridium compound in the formic acid disproportionation process, leading to methanol production, he demonstrated the potential for high yields and achieved yields of up to 75% in [[deuterium]] oxide (D<sub>2</sub>O) through this process.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2017/gc/c6gc03359h|title=Aqueous phase homogeneous formic acid disproportionation into methanol|first1=K.|last1=Sordakis|first2=A.|last2=Tsurusaki|first3=M.|last3=Iguchi|first4=H.|last4=Kawanami|first5=Y.|last5=Himeda|first6=G.|last6=Laurenczy|date=May 22, 2017|journal=Green Chemistry|volume=19|issue=10|pages=2371–2378|doi=10.1039/C6GC03359H|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Reaction mechanisms===
Laurenczy's research on reaction mechanisms has resulted in an improved understanding of catalytic reactions<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2004/cc/b401537a|title=Carbon monoxide solubility in ionic liquids: determination, prediction and relevance to hydroformylation|first1=C. André|last1=Ohlin|first2=Paul J.|last2=Dyson|first3=Gábor|last3=Laurenczy|date=April 28, 2004|journal=Chemical Communications|issue=9|pages=1070–1071|doi=10.1039/B401537A|pmid=15116189 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> and synthetic methodologies, including the design of efficient and selective transformations, as well as the synthesis of complex molecules with applications in medicine,<ref>{{Cite journal|title=In vitro and in vivo evaluation of ruthenium(II)-arene PTA complexes|first1=Claudine|last1=Scolaro|first2=Alberta|last2=Bergamo|first3=Laura|last3=Brescacin|first4=Riccarda|last4=Delfino|first5=Moreno|last5=Cocchietto|first6=Gábor|last6=Laurenczy|first7=Tilmann J.|last7=Geldbach|first8=Gianni|last8=Sava|first9=Paul J.|last9=Dyson|date=June 16, 2005|journal=Journal of Medicinal Chemistry|volume=48|issue=12|pages=4161–4171|doi=10.1021/jm050015d|pmid=15943488}}</ref> materials science.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1993/c3/c39930000187|title=Aqueous catalytic dimerisation of ethylene: characterization of the reaction intermediates [Ru(CH2CH2)(H2O)5](tos)2 and [Ru(CH2CH2)2(H2O)4](tos)2(tos = toluene-p-sulfonate)|first1=G.|last1=Laurenczy|first2=A. E.|last2=Merbach|date=January 1, 1993|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Chemical Communications|issue=2|pages=187–189|doi=10.1039/C39930000187|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000326709700696X|title=A new variable temperature and pressure infrared cell to study liquid and liquid–gas systems|first1=Gábor|last1=Laurenczy|first2=Ferenc|last2=Lukács|first3=Raymond|last3=Roulet|date=February 27, 1998|journal=Analytica Chimica Acta|volume=359|issue=3|pages=275–281|doi=10.1016/S0003-2670(97)00696-X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Moreover, his examination of aqueous catalytic reactions demonstrated successful transmission of carbon dioxide into formic acid and methanol utilizing an iridium complex within an aqueous medium, while operating under ambient temperatures.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/chem.201603407|title=Carbon Dioxide to Methanol: The Aqueous Catalytic Way at Room Temperature|first1=Katerina|last1=Sordakis|first2=Akihiro|last2=Tsurusaki|first3=Masayuki|last3=Iguchi|first4=Hajime|last4=Kawanami|first5=Yuichiro|last5=Himeda|first6=Gábor|last6=Laurenczy|date=October 24, 2016|journal=Chemistry - A European Journal|volume=22|issue=44|pages=15605–15608|doi=10.1002/chem.201603407|pmid=27582027 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>
